why: California's constitution has never authorised sports betting of any kind. Article IV, Section 19 hands out gambling permissions one at a time - a state lottery in subdivision (d), charitable bingo in (c), horse racing in (b), tribal casino compacts in (f) - and sports wagering is simply not on the list, while subdivision (e) says the Legislature "has no power to authorize, and shall prohibit, casinos of the type currently operating in Nevada and New Jersey." Taking or placing a sports bet is a crime under Penal Code 337a, which covers "pool selling or bookmaking, with or without writing, at any time or place" and carries up to a year in jail and a $5,000 fine. Voters were given the chance to change this in November 2022 and refused twice: Proposition 26, for in-person tribal sportsbooks, lost 67.0% to 33.0%, and Proposition 27, for online and mobile sports betting, lost 82.3% to 17.7%.
legalToday: Tribal casinos (66 of them, under compacts with 79 tribes as of the 2022 Legislative Analyst's count), 84 licensed card rooms, the California State Lottery, and pari-mutuel betting on horse racing. Card rooms, tribal gaming and third-party proposition player services are licensed by the California Gambling Control Commission, with the Department of Justice Bureau of Gambling Control handling compliance inspections and approving every card room game before it can be offered. Online casino games are not licensed at all, and since AB 831 took effect (chaptered 11 October 2025) Penal Code 337o makes it "unlawful for any person or entity to operate, conduct, or offer an online sweepstakes game in this state," which shuts the door on sweepstakes-model online casinos.

why: Hawaii has no gambling law to license an online sportsbook under - beyond the criminal code it has no gambling law at all. HRS 712-1220 defines gambling as staking something of value "upon the outcome of a contest of chance or a future contingent event not under his control or influence," which is exactly what a sports bet is, and HRS 712-1223 makes knowingly participating in any gambling activity a misdemeanour. Running a book is treated far more harshly: under HRS 712-1222 even negligently advancing or profiting from gambling activity is a class C felony, and HRS 712-1221 makes bookmaking above five bets totalling more than $500 in any seven-day period a class B felony. The only softening anywhere in the chapter is the "social gambling" affirmative defence in HRS 712-1231, and that defence is expressly unavailable when "the gambling activity is bookmaking."

why: Idaho's constitution bans gambling outright rather than merely leaving it unauthorised. Article III, Section 20 says gambling "is contrary to public policy and is strictly prohibited" apart from three named exceptions - a state lottery, pari-mutuel betting and charitable bingo and raffles - and subsection (2) adds that none of those exceptions may "employ any form of casino gambling" or "any electronic or electromechanical imitation or simulation of any form of casino gambling." Sports betting is not one of the three exceptions, and Idaho Code 18-3801 removes any doubt by defining gambling to include risking money on "the happening or outcome of an event, including a sporting event." Placing a bet is a misdemeanour under Idaho Code 18-3802 and taking bets is separately punished as bookmaking or pool selling under Idaho Code 18-3809.
legalToday: Three things, exactly as the constitution lists them. The Idaho Lottery (Idaho Code Title 67, Chapter 74) runs the state lottery and also licenses charitable bingo and raffle organisations through its Charitable Gaming programme. Pari-mutuel horse race betting is allowed by Idaho Code 54-2512, which legalises pari-mutuel wagering and declares other betting illegal, and is overseen by the Idaho State Racing Commission, a division of the Idaho State Police. Separately, Idaho Code 67-429B provides that "Indian tribes are authorized to conduct gaming using tribal video gaming machines pursuant to state-tribal gaming compacts which specifically permit their use," and that such a machine "may be used to conduct gaming only by an Indian tribe."

why: No authorized sports betting of any kind, retail or online. The Department of Public Safety Alcohol and Gambling Enforcement Division lists the state's legal gambling as charitable gambling, the Minnesota Lottery, pari-mutuel horse racing, card rooms and tribal Class III casino games, and lists sports betting among the illegal activities it criminally investigates. Tribal Class III gaming runs under 22 tribal-state compacts with 11 Tribal Nations covering 20 casinos; per DPS the Class III games permitted under those compacts are blackjack and video games of chance, and the compacts have no expiration date (https://dps.mn.gov/divisions/age/gambling/tribal-state-gaming-compacts). Any legalisation therefore has to be negotiated around tribal exclusivity, which is the fault line the bills below keep failing on. Bills carry over within the 94th Legislature (2025-2026 biennium). No online casino / iGaming bill exists at all: exact-phrase searches of bill text on revisor.mn.gov for 'online casino', 'internet casino', 'internet gaming', 'interactive gaming' and 'iGaming' return no House or Senate documents. Minnesota does not record a 'died in committee' status, so a bill's status is simply its last recorded action.

why: Montana's only legal sports betting is Sports Bet Montana, run by the Montana Lottery, and the geofencing is written into statute rather than left to regulation. MCA 23-7-104 makes the operation of sports wagering lawful only as it pertains to the state lottery. MCA 23-7-103(11) defines a sports wagering license as authorizing wagering conducted through mobile application or other digital platforms only where it is 'initiated and received or otherwise made exclusively within the physical confines using location-based services of the single approved sports wagering facility', and 23-7-103(10) defines that facility as an approved lottery location licensed as a gambling operator. So the Sports Bet Montana app exists but is geofenced to licensed premises, and is not statewide online sports betting. The legislature is biennial: the 69th Regular Session (2025) is the most recent session with introduced bills, and there is no 2026 session. Montana moved in the RESTRICTIVE direction in 2025: SB 555 revised the definition of internet gambling to include online casinos, brought cryptocurrency into the definition of internet gambling and raised criminal penalties; it was signed by the Governor on 2025-05-13 and had a chapter number assigned 2025-05-16 (https://bills.legmt.gov/#/laws/bill/2/2671). A 2027-session draft request, LC0032 'Generally revise laws relating to sport betting', exists in the legislature's bill system but has no bill number, status or action date, so it is not recorded as a bill.

why: New Mexico has NO state authorizing statute for sports betting at all. Sports betting exists purely under Class III tribal gaming compacts, on-site at tribal casinos. The Office of the State Gaming Representative told the Legislature's Indian Affairs Committee on 2025-09-25, in a handout published on nmlegis.gov, that sports betting is limited to on-site wagering only at tribal casinos chosen to open sportsbooks, that New Mexico law has not legalized either retail or online wagering elsewhere, and that only eight casinos currently offer sports betting. The same handout shows the compacts anticipate but do not permit internet gaming: if internet gaming is authorized within the State, the State and the Tribe agree to reopen good faith negotiations to evaluate its impact and consider adjustments to the Compact. This is tribal-compact exclusivity in its purest form, and it means any online expansion is a compact renegotiation rather than a simple bill. Nothing is moving legislatively: the 2026 Regular Session is a 30-day session constitutionally limited under Art. 4, Sec. 5(B) to budget, appropriations and revenue bills, bills drawn pursuant to special messages of the governor, and previously vetoed bills; its full official listing of 812 measures contains not one with gaming, gambling, wagering, betting or casino in the title. The 2025 60-day session had eleven gaming bills, but all concerned Gaming Control Board administration, gaming machine standards, horse racing, racetrack licensing or gaming tax, none online.

Texas meets in odd years only: the most recent regular session was the 89th Regular (2025) and there is no 2026 regular session. Two 2025 called sessions were held and the Texas Legislature Online 'Bills By Subject / GAMBLING' report returns 'There are no bills on this subject for this legislative session' for both. why: Sports betting is legal but TRIBAL ONLY and on-premises, under Class III compacts. RCW 9.46.0364 permits a tribe's compact to be amended to authorize sports wagering 'on Indian lands'. RCW 9.46.0368 authorizes transmission of gambling information over the internet for that wagering only provided the wager may be placed and accepted at a tribe's gaming facility while the customer is physically present on the premises. The Washington State Gambling Commission states that ESHB 2638 authorizes sports wagering on a very limited basis by restricting it to tribal casinos, that the sportsbook must be located within a tribe's gaming facility, and that each gaming operation must use a geofence to ensure patrons can only place mobile sports wagers while physically on the premises. Online gambling outside that authorization is a CLASS C FELONY: RCW 9.46.240 makes knowingly transmitting or receiving gambling information by the internet a class C felony under RCW 9A.20.021. Nothing is moving toward online: all 3,757 bill numbers in the 2025-26 biennium were pulled from the Legislature's own web service and filtered; the complete gambling-related set is 11 bills and none authorizes online or mobile wagering off tribal property, and none concerns online casino. Note that the one enacted 2026 sports-wagering bill reinforces rather than loosens the restriction: SB 6137, 'Concerning the regulated sports wagering industry', was signed by the Governor as Chapter 246, 2026 Laws on 2026-03-30; it permits wagering on collegiate events involving Washington post-secondary institutions at tribal facilities and bars prop bets on those athletes, amending RCW 9.46.0368 while KEEPING the physical-presence requirement (https://app.leg.wa.gov/billsummary?BillNumber=6137&Year=2026&Initiative=False). Wisconsin sports betting is tribal: 2025 Wisconsin Act 247 (2025 Assembly Bill 601, published 10 April 2026) creates s. 945.01 (1) (h) excluding from the criminal definition of 'bet' an event or sports wager 'made by a person physically located in this state using a mobile or other electronic device if the server or other device used to conduct such event or sports wager is physically located on a federally recognized American Indian tribe's Indian lands' under a pre-1 April 1993 IGRA compact. Wagering is therefore offered by tribes under tribal/state compacts, not under state operator licences, and there is no state licensee list at all. The Division of Gaming's own page describes its role as protecting 'the integrity of Indian and charitable gaming' through licensing, background investigations and enforcement, and its Office of Indian Gaming and Regulatory Compliance regulates tribal casinos; the page does not mention sports wagering.
